name: Cantonese written in Jyutping
variety: Hong Kong Cantonese; the same spoken language and the same sounds as yue, written in the Jyutping romanisation of the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong instead of Han characters
sources: Zee, Eric (1999). Chinese (Hong Kong Cantonese). In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press, 58-60.
Bauer, Robert S. & Benedict, Paul K. (1997). Modern Cantonese Phonology. Mouton de Gruyter.
Matthews, Stephen & Yip, Virginia (2011). Cantonese: A Comprehensive Grammar, 2nd edition. Routledge.
Chen, Matthew Y. (2000). Tone Sandhi: Patterns across Chinese Dialects. Cambridge University Press.
Yu, Alan C. L. (2007). Understanding near mergers: the case of morphological tone in Cantonese. Phonology 24, 187-214.
Lisker, Leigh & Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20, 384-422.
Mok, Peggy P. K. (2009). On the syllable-timing of Cantonese and Beijing Mandarin. Chinese Journal of Phonetics 2.
Mok, Peggy P. K., Zuo, Donghui & Wong, Peggy W. Y. (2013). Production and perception of a sound change in progress: tone merging in Hong Kong Cantonese. Language Variation and Change 25.

Wong, Wai Yi P., Chan, Marjorie K. M. & Beckman, Mary E. (2005). An autosegmental-metrical analysis and prosodic annotation conventions for Cantonese. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology. Oxford University Press.
Ma, Joan K.-Y., Ciocca, Valter & Whitehill, Tara L. (2006). Effect of intonation on Cantonese lexical tones. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 120.
Yu, Kristine M. & Lam, Hiu Wai (2014). The role of creaky voice in Cantonese tonal perception. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 136.
contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated in stops and affricates; Jyutping writes the unaspirated series b d g gw z and the aspirated series p t k kw c, and neither series is voiced
labialised versus plain velar stops (gw, kw against g, k)
long aː (Jyutping aa) versus short ɐ (Jyutping a) in closed syllables and diphthongs (saam1 against sam1, gaai1 against gai1)
six tones, written with the digits 1 to 6 after the syllable
three final nasals m n ng and three unreleased final stops p t k
front rounded vowels yu, oe and eo
two syllabic nasals, m and ng
allophony: Jyutping i is [iː], but [ɪ] before k and ng; u is [uː], but [ʊ] before k and ng; oe is [œː]; eo is [ɵ] and occurs only before t, n and i (eoi is [ɵy]); e is [ɛː], but [e] in ei; o is [ɔː], but [o] in ou
Jyutping j is the glide [j], z is [ts], c is [tsʰ]; yu is the vowel [yː]
final p t k have no audible release and are glottally reinforced
z c s move toward alveolo-palatal before the front rounded vowels
initial n is replaced by l by most younger Hong Kong speakers; initial ng is variably dropped; syllabic ng is often replaced by syllabic m
gw and kw lose their rounding before o for many speakers
zero-initial syllables begin with a glottal stop
syllable_structure: (C)V(C) plus tone, or a syllabic nasal plus tone; the coda is one of m n ŋ p t k or an offglide i, u or y
phonotactics: no consonant clusters (kʷ and kʷʰ are single consonants)
codas are limited to m n ŋ p t k and the offglides
checked syllables (ending in p t k) carry only tones 1, 3 and 6, realised short as 5, 3 and 2
long vowels are followed by short codas and short vowels by long codas, so rhyme duration is roughly constant

stress.rule: Every syllable carries a full lexical tone and full vowel; there is no neutral tone and no stress placement rule.
stress.cues: prominence for focus is carried by lengthening and expanded pitch range, not by a stress accent

rhythm.notes: More evenly syllable-timed than Beijing Mandarin (Mok 2009).

length.notes: Length is contrastive only for the low vowels, aa against a, and is tied to quality. A short vowel is followed by a longer coda, so the rhyme as a whole keeps about the same duration.

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; declination across the utterance and lowering of the last syllable; sentence-final particles with their own tones carry much of the sentence-type meaning
intonation.yes_no_question: usually marked by a particle (maa3, aa4, me1) or by A-not-A form; a question without a particle has a high rising boundary tone on the last syllable, so that every tone ends high (Ma, Ciocca & Whitehill 2006)
intonation.wh_question: statement-like declination; often ends in the particle aa3 or ne1
intonation.continuation: level or slightly raised end of the phrase with lengthening of the last syllable, then pitch reset
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; boundary tones on the final syllable are added to the lexical tone (Wong, Chan & Beckman 2005)

inventory.name: tone 1, high level (Jyutping digit 1)
inventory.description: High level, with a non-contrastive high falling variant 53. In checked syllables short, 5.

inventory.name: tone 2, high rising (Jyutping digit 2)
inventory.description: Rise from low-mid to high, also written 35. Also the shape of the changed tone, which Jyutping writes as 2 when it is shown.
inventory.duration: slightly longer than the level tones

inventory.name: tone 3, mid level (Jyutping digit 3)
inventory.description: Mid level. In checked syllables short, 3, mostly with long vowels.

inventory.name: tone 4, low falling (Jyutping digit 4)
inventory.description: Low falling to the bottom of the range, also described as extra low level 11.
inventory.phonation: modal, often creaky toward the end (Yu & Lam 2014)

inventory.name: tone 5, low rising (Jyutping digit 5)
inventory.description: Rise from low to mid, also written 13.
inventory.duration: slightly longer than the level tones

inventory.name: tone 6, low level (Jyutping digit 6)
inventory.description: Low level, about one step below tone 3. In checked syllables short, 2.

sandhi: no productive, phonologically conditioned tone sandhi in present-day Hong Kong Cantonese

changed tone (pinjam), lexically and morphologically conditioned: a syllable with a non-high tone takes a high rising tone like tone 2, or in some words high level 55; Jyutping text normally writes the tone as spoken (jan2 in naam4 jan2, waa2 in gwong2 dung1 waa2), so nothing has to be derived by a reader
intonational boundary tones change the end of the last syllable's tone, most clearly the high rise of particle-less questions
tone.neutral_tone: none; every syllable, including particles, carries a full tone
tone.notes: Jyutping has no digit for the high falling variant 53; eSpeak NG's tone phoneme 7 (53) can be reached by typing the digit 7. Tone mergers in progress among younger speakers: 2 with 5, 3 with 6, 4 with 6 (Mok, Zuo & Wong 2013).

phonation: creaky voice at the end of the low falling tone 4
glottal reinforcement of the unreleased final stops
no phonation contrast in consonants; aspiration only

problems: the syllabic nasals lose their syllable and their tone: m4 and ng5 come out as a bare consonant (m, N) with no tone, and hm4, hng6 likewise
a syllable typed without a tone digit is given tone 1 (nei hou is spoken with two high level tones)
every Latin word is read as Jyutping, so English words inside the text are read letter by letter as Cantonese syllables
the unaspirated stops b d g gw are spoken with the voiced stops of the base table instead of voiceless unaspirated stops
the affricates differ in place instead of aspiration: z uses the alveolar affricate recording ustop/ts, c uses the palato-alveolar recording ustop/tsh
no sentence intonation and no declination: CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c ignores the clause type, and nei5 hou2 maa3? gives the same pitch as a statement
the tonal pitch range is very small: the six tones lie between about 76 and 98 Hz at the default voice pitch (about 4.4 semitones, measured on the output); tones 3 and 6 are one semitone apart

the finals ing, ung, eng, oeng, ang are built from a vowel plus the consonant N, while Han-character input uses the single rhyme phonemes ing, ung, eng, oeng, ang of the phoneme table, so the same word can sound different in the two scripts
checked syllables are not shortened beyond the inherent length of the vowel; no creaky phonation on tone 4; rising tones are not longer than level tones
a short pause between words ('words 1') and no tonal coarticulation
good: Jyutping with tone digits is read directly, syllable by syllable, including multi-syllable words typed without spaces (jyut6ping3)
the six tones have the right shapes and relative heights
long aa and short a differ in both quality and length; final p t k are silent closures with formant transitions
the lax allophones of i and u before k and ng are chosen by the phoneme table

notes: The voice also reads Han characters through the same dictionary as yue. As in other Latin-script voices, a full stop ends the sentence only when the next word begins with a capital letter.
